query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an approximately 50 nm yttria (Y2O3) coating on the surface of refractory high-entropy alloys via atomic layer deposition will form a more adherent and protective oxide scale that slows oxygen diffusion and reduces oxidation under extreme high-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) that exhibits rapid oxidation and scale spallation when exposed to oxygen-rich environments at high temperatures (e.g., 1100–1200°C).
generation.intervention: A single, isolated intervention using a thin, conformal ALD-deposited yttria (Y2O3) coating (~50 nm thick) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1150°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., pure oxygen or controlled high oxygen partial pressure) for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform Y2O3 surface layer that acts as a reactive element source, facilitating the formation of a continuous and adherent protective oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The Y2O3 coating provides a reactive element effect that promotes the formation and adhesion of a slow-growing, oxygen-resistant scale by inhibiting oxygen ingress and enhancing oxide scale cohesiveness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ALD yttria-coated alloy is expected to show a significantly reduced mass gain due to oxidation and improved scale adherence compared to the untreated alloy, indicating enhanced high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated RHEA exhibits rapid oxidation with a high mass gain (e.g., >120 mg/cm² over 100 hours) and considerable oxide spallation under the specified test conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is limited to scenarios where the coating remains defect-free and interfaces well with the alloy; extreme deviations in temperature, prolonged exposure beyond 100 hours, or environments with additional corrosive species may diminish the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: While reactive element additions have shown benefits in simpler alloy systems, the exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance for refractory HEAs with an ALD Y2O3 coating is uncertain and may vary with coating quality and alloy surface characteristics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA samples: one set with an approximately 50 nm ALD-deposited Y2O3 coating and one set as the untreated control. Expose both sets to 1150°C in a controlled oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours. After exposure, analyze the samples using mass gain measurements, cross-sectional microscopy of the oxide scale, and adhesion tests (e.g., spallation analysis) to assess the protective quality of the oxide layer.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM/TEM
Adhesion/spallation behavior of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD Y2O3-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in mass gain or improvement in oxide scale adherence compared to the untreated control under identical test conditions, the hypothesis that the Y2O3 coating improves high-temperature oxygen resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. frame.system: Refractory high-entropy alloys designed for structural applications at extreme temperatures. The starting state is an untreated HEA that exhibits rapid oxidation (oxygen attack) under high-temperature service conditions.
frame.goal: Improve the high‐temperature oxygen resistance of the alloy to ensure longevity and structural integrity under extreme temperature exposures.
frame.limitation: The current alloy formulation is insufficient in resisting high-temperature oxidation, leading to rapid degradation when exposed to oxygen-rich atmospheres at elevated temperatures.
constraints: only a single intervention is allowed
the intervention must yield a measurable improvement relative to the untreated alloy

the hypothesis should be falsifiable via a clear experimental outcome
supporting prior evidence must be cited to justify the intervention
frame.regime: The intervention is anticipated to be effective under extreme-temperature test conditions (e.g., 1100–1200°C) in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (either pure oxygen or a controlled oxygen partial pressure) with extended exposure (e.g., 100 hours) to simulate service conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous studies in oxidation resistance have employed multi-element modifications and surface coatings, but these often involved multiple concurrent interventions that complicated interpretation and durability assessments.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on refractory and high‐entropy alloys have tried to improve high‐temperature performance indirectly by incorporating in‐situ formed oxide or carbide phases (as in the NbMoCrTiAl system from PMC7513042) and by studying oxidation mechanisms in classical HEAs (as in PMC10384371). In many cases, reactive element additions (e.g., yttrium or hafnium) were used in simpler alloys to promote formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale, but those approaches were bundled with other alloy modifications, complicating clear attribution of the oxidation resistance. The work has evolved from creating multiphase composites for strength and oxidation resistance toward investigating the detailed scale formation and adhesion mechanisms. However, a single, isolated intervention that reliably generates a protective oxide under extreme temperature and oxygen-rich conditions in refractory high-entropy alloys remains unproven.
decision.unsolved: A standalone intervention that promotes the formation of a durable, slow-growing, oxygen‐resistant scale under service conditions (e.g., 1100–1200°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for ~100 hours) has not been demonstrated in refractory HEAs. The gap is to isolate the reactive element effect without modifying the bulk composition or introducing multiple phases, and to clearly link the intervention to improved oxidation kinetics and scale adhesion.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, conformal layer (approximately 50 nm) of yttria (Y2O3) using atomic layer deposition (ALD) onto the alloy surface
decision.why: Using a surface coating allows isolation of the reactive element effect – a mechanism known to enhance oxide scale adhesion and inhibit oxygen diffusion – without altering the bulk alloy composition. This approach follows the trend where reactive element effects improved oxidation resistance, as observed in simpler systems, and meets the design cues for a single, measurable intervention under extreme conditions.
